greek.title: The Sacred Rights of the Stranger
greek.body:
When Odysseus washed ashore on Phaeacia, naked and exhausted, Princess Nausicaa recognized her duty before asking his name. She offered clothes, food, and safe passage—the obligations of xenia, guest-friendship, which bound Greek households to strangers who crossed their threshold.

This wasn't mere hospitality. Zeus himself bore the epithet Xenios, protector of strangers, and to turn away a suppliant risked divine wrath. Every xenos carried potential: he might be a god in disguise, testing mortal virtue, or a powerful ally whose reciprocal friendship could span generations. The Athenians formalized this with proxenoi, citizens who represented foreign states and housed their visitors.

Yet xenos cuts both ways—stranger and guest-friend share the same word. The Greek world knew that the foreigner at your door embodied both threat and promise, demanding a calculated generosity that balanced fear with hope.
